newsitem.title: USA: U.S. turns cold on Belgrade's Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: U.S. turns cold on Belgrade's Milosevic.

text.p: The United States wined and dined Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic last year in the run-up to the Dayton agreement ending Bosnia's 43-month war.
But now the Americans, with uncertain consequences for the Bosnia peace deal and for Serbia, are backing his vociferous political opponents who are staging daily marches through the Belgrade streets.
In recent days, Secretary of State Warren Christopher and other senior U.S. officials have sought to isolate Milosevic from the international acceptance he had begun to reclaim.

They have bluntly accused him of dictatorship, threatened him with a reimposition of U.N. sanctions if he uses force against protestors and cancelled a meeting scheduled between him and a senior U.S. official.

The Americans have also demanded he open a dialogue with political opponents -- a kind of intervention in Serbia's internal affairs they have refused to apply to many other countries whose domestic policies they oppose.

The change marks another twist in the U.S. relationship with Milosevic, who in the early years of the war was widely condemned as the most brutal military force in the conflict because of his crucial support for Bosnian Serbs.

In 1992, after evidence emerged that the Bosnian Serbs committed mass kilings and "ethnic cleansing," then Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger said Milosevic and others should be tried for "crimes against humanity."

But in late 1995, when a Bosnia peace agreement looked possible, Washington embraced Milosevic as a partner in the negotiations, believing only the Serbian leader could bring Bosnian Serbs to the table and force them to commit.

Milosevic did just that. He has been relied on since then, with mixed results, to keep the Bosnian Serbs in line with the peace deal agreed in Dayton, Ohio, on November 25, 1995. Implementation of key aspects of the accords led the United Nations to lift economic sanctions which had hurt Serbia.

But Washington, insisting on keeping some leverage, has unilaterally retained the "outer wall" of sanctions, blocking Belgrade's entry into world institutions like the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

U.S. officials are determined to continue the sanctions indefinitely. They also hold out the possibility of reimposing the U.N. sanctions, although opposition from Russia and other countries makes that unlikely.

Susan Woodward, a Balkans expert with the independent Brookings Institution says that while U.S. pressure on Milosevic is important as a moral stick, only Europe has the carrots to persuade MIlosevic to move toward democracy.
The Europeans have been in trade negotiations with Serbia and control membership in the organisations Milosevic most wants his country to join, like the European Union, she said.

For this reason, she and other experts believe only a joint effort between the United States and Europe could have effective influence on Milosevic. Christopher pursued that at a NATO foreign ministers meeting in Brussels this week.
The Belgrade protests began three weeks ago when Milosevic's socialist government annulled local election victories, including in Belgrade, by the opposition.

Foreign policy expert Richard Haass said that when the protests began Washington initially seemed "reluctant to let go of Milosevic for fear that (it would) jeopardise Dayton or possibly contribute to a process which could bring to power nationalists who might be as big or a bigger problem."
But Haass, former adviser to President George Bush, said that "even now Milosevic's cooperation with Dayton is limited" and the U.S. decision to take a tough line was appropriate.
U.S. officials acknowledge uncertainties about how their strategy will play out. Milosevic could end cooperation with the Bosnia peace deal, as he has before, they said.
One knowledgeable official told Reuters "there is no question Milosevic is (politically) wounded" by the prolonged protests and has been "sobered" by the experience.
But as for whether Milosevic might use force to subdue the protests or be overthrown, the official said: "We don't know. Almost anything could happen there."

With the political unrest now in Belgrade, concerns about broader stability in the Balkans has seized the stage. In Croatia, President Franjo Tudjman, another key signer of the Dayton agreement, has what U.S. officials say is incurable stomach cancer.
